blueprint_topic: Standard and Contact Precautions for fecal-oral infection risk
stem: An adult hospitalized with hepatitis A has fecal incontinence. Which infection-control plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Use Contact Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions, with meticulous hand hygiene and measures to prevent fecal contamination of the environment.
options.B: Use Standard Precautions only because hepatitis A never requires additional transmission-based precautions in adults.
options.C: Use Airborne Precautions because hepatitis A is primarily spread by inhalation of respiratory aerosols.
options.D: Use Droplet Precautions because hepatitis A is primarily transmitted by respiratory secretions during coughing and sneezing.

rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies hepatitis A as primarily transmitted by the fecal-oral route. In CDC Appendix A, viral hepatitis A generally requires Standard Precautions, but diapered or incontinent patients require Contact Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions. CDC also notes that healthcare-associated hepatitis A transmission has been associated with fecal incontinence and inadequate hand hygiene, making meticulous hand hygiene and environmental contamination control directly relevant in this scenario. B is incorrect because fecal incontinence is the specific condition that changes the precaution requirement from Standard alone to Contact plus Standard. C and D are incorrect because hepatitis A is not primarily transmitted by airborne or respiratory-droplet routes. The final item deliberately includes fecal incontinence in the stem so that Contact Precautions are uniquely indicated rather than creating ambiguity with uncomplicated hepatitis A, for which Standard Precautions are generally sufficient.
educational_objective: Apply CDC isolation guidance by using Contact plus Standard Precautions for a hospitalized patient with hepatitis A who is fecally incontinent, while reinforcing hand hygiene and fecal-contamination control because HAV is transmitted primarily by the fecal-oral route.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions Recommended for Selected Infections and Conditions; Clinical Overview of Hepatitis A; Hepatitis A Prevention and Control
source_version_date: CDC Appendix A current web version accessed 2026-08-18; Clinical Overview of Hepatitis A updated 2025-08-29; Hepatitis A Prevention and Control updated 2025-01-31
source_locator: CDC Infection Control, Appendix A → Hepatitis, viral Type A: Standard Precautions; Hepatitis, viral Type A—Diapered or incontinent patients: Contact + Standard. CDC Clinical Overview of Hepatitis A → Key points/Overview: HAV spreads primarily through fecal-oral transmission. CDC Hepatitis A Prevention and Control → Good hygiene: wash hands with soap and water after bathroom use, caring for an infected person, or changing diapers. CDC ACIP 2020 appendices → healthcare-setting section: transmission outbreaks associated with fecal incontinence and inadequate hand hygiene; Contact Precautions for diapered or incontinent patients, Standard Precautions for others.
source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports fecal-oral transmission of HAV, Standard Precautions for uncomplicated hepatitis A, Contact plus Standard Precautions for diapered or incontinent hepatitis A patients, and the importance of hand hygiene and control of fecal contamination in healthcare settings.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment → Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: entry-level nursing activities involving infection-prevention practices, standard/transmission-based precautions, and protection of clients and healthcare personnel from communicable-disease exposure.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source recall item into an applied CDC isolation decision. The final stem adds fecal incontinence, which is the condition that makes Contact plus Standard Precautions uniquely correct; it distinguishes this from uncomplicated hepatitis A, for which Standard Precautions are generally sufficient. Weak transmission-route distractors were rewritten to test actual precaution selection, and the rationale preserves the fecal-oral and hand-hygiene teaching without overgeneralizing Contact Precautions to every patient with hepatitis A.
audit_findings: The source item correctly identified fecal-oral transmission but remained a low-level recall question and did not distinguish Standard from Contact Precautions in healthcare.
Fresh CDC review confirms that hepatitis A generally requires Standard Precautions, while diapered or incontinent patients require Contact plus Standard Precautions.
CDC independently confirms that HAV is primarily fecal-oral and that healthcare transmission has been associated with fecal incontinence and inadequate hand hygiene.
The final stem contains fecal incontinence so Contact plus Standard is uniquely indicated; without this qualifier, Standard Precautions alone could be correct and the item would be ambiguous.
